title: Lay out and test a CMOS inverter
concept: The PMOS and NMOS occupy separate rows. Their drains meet on Y, and their bodies reach the two power rails through the terminal contacts.
question: Which physical connection joins the two drains?
explanation: Y connects both drain contacts through Metal 2 drops and vias to its shared Metal 3 track.
focus: Trace the A drops to the two gates and Y to the two drains. Each body contact should reach its own rail.
reflection: Explain how the Y route joins the drain contacts. Compare the schematic and layout-loaded waveforms and report the extra estimated load on Y.

title: Lay out and test a two-input NAND
concept: The NMOS stack has an internal diffusion connection called N_STACK. Separate contacts let you see which nets reach the cell pins and which stay inside it.
question: Which connection stays internal to the NAND cell?
explanation: N_STACK joins the two NMOS devices. The output is low only at A=1 and B=1.
focus: Trace the NMOS series path from Y to N_STACK to VGND. N_STACK has a Metal 3 track without a left-edge port.
reflection: Show where N_STACK stays internal and which input vector pulls Y down. Describe how series devices and added metal capacitance affect the falling edge.

title: Lay out and test a two-input NOR
concept: The PMOS pull-up uses a series connection. Its internal P_STACK track must remain separate from the upper supply rail.
question: Where does P_STACK connect in the layout?
explanation: P_STACK joins the PMOS stack. Both PMOS gates must be low for the stack to charge Y.
focus: Follow VPWR into the upper row, then trace P_STACK between the PMOS devices and Y at the far side of the stack.
reflection: Compare the NOR pull-up layout with the NAND pull-down layout. Identify the vector that charges Y and note the layout-added load.

title: Lay out and test an AND-OR-invert cell
concept: AOI21 merges two distinct pull-down paths at Y. C drives a direct branch and the A/B path uses a series stack.
question: Which routed input alone should force Y low?
explanation: A high on C enables a direct pull-down branch to VGND and blocks the complementary pull-up.
focus: Follow the C track to both device rows. Identify P_BRANCH and N_STACK under the output routes.
reflection: Trace the branch that lets C override A and B. Use one captured vector and the routed output load to explain the observed transition.

title: Lay out and test a transmission-gate multiplexer
concept: The transmission gates need separate S and S_B conductors. Metal 2 drops cross Metal 3 tracks, with a via only where they connect.
question: What connects a Metal 2 drop to a crossing Metal 3 track?
options: A via between the two layers
explanation: A via makes the layer transition. The separated S and S_B nets control which data input reaches the buffered output.
focus: Locate the S and S_B tracks and the internal SELECTED node. Check where the output buffer drives Y.
reflection: Compare S and S_B routes and show how each data input reaches Y. Compare a switching edge in the two saved models.

title: Lay out and test a rising-edge D flip-flop
concept: The master and slave latches use CLK and CLK_B on distinct conductors. Q also feeds back into the slave latch, so the output route connects an internal path and the external pin.
question: Which pair of clock tracks needs separate routing?
explanation: The complementary CLK and CLK_B tracks enable different paths on each phase. Q captures on the rising edge and holds between edges.
focus: Follow CLK and CLK_B through the large cell. Locate the Q track where the slave output and feedback meet.
reflection: Use the layout and the captured samples to explain how Q feeds the slave loop, captures on rising edges, and holds when D changes.

title: Fit an inverter into a 12.8 µm cell
concept: Neighboring cells share the same rail heights. Reduce the horizontal device pitch so this inverter fits its width budget and still switches correctly.
question: Which edit reduces the cell width while leaving the shared rail heights fixed?
explanation: A smaller device pitch brings the two device columns closer together. The boundary and routing still have to pass the physical checks.
focus: Measure the 13.8 µm starter outline. Change the horizontal pitch and compare the revised boundary.
tune: Reduce Horizontal device pitch, rebuild the layout, and finish the missing routes again.
solution: Set Horizontal device pitch to 4.8 µm. The footprint is 12.8 µm wide. Both input levels must still pass with the 10 fF fixture.
reflection: Record the starter and final widths. Explain how you reduced the width while keeping the same power-rail heights and passing the logic test.

title: Drive 40 fF with a faster NAND
concept: A NAND discharges through two series NMOS devices. With A held high, the rising B edge isolates the delay through this path into a 40 fF load.
question: Which change directly reduces resistance in the loaded NAND pull-down?
explanation: Wider devices reduce channel resistance. The loaded B-to-Y edge measures whether the pull-down is fast enough.
focus: Locate MN_A and MN_B on the N_STACK path from Y to VGND.
tune: Increase the NMOS stack width, rebuild, and rerun the 40 fF test.
solution: Set NMOS stack width to 2 µm. At the applied 40 fF load, check that B rising to Y falling takes at most 100 ps and all four logic vectors pass.
reflection: Record the delay before and after sizing the series pair. Explain why the test holds A high while B switches.

title: Meet the flip-flop clock-to-Q budget
concept: The Q inverter must drive 40 fF within a clock-to-output delay budget. The combined output-driver width limits how much you can enlarge the two devices.
question: Which input transition starts the clock-to-Q delay measurement?
options: The rising clock crossing at half the supply
A falling D edge while the clock is high
explanation: Start at the rising clock crossing and stop at the corresponding Q crossing. Measure rising and falling Q separately.
focus: Find the Q driver, MN_Q and MP_Q, at the end of the slave latch.
tune: Adjust the two Q driver widths separately. Check both clock-to-Q delay readings and their combined width before rerunning.
solution: Set the Q NMOS width to 2 µm and the Q PMOS width to 3.5 µm. The combined width is 5.5 µm. Verify Q rise at or below 185 ps and Q fall at or below 128 ps, with capture and hold intact.
reflection: Record both clock-to-Q measurements and your combined driver width. Explain how you divided the width budget between the NMOS and PMOS.

title: Make two cells fit side by side
concept: Check how independently routed cells share power where their boundaries meet. Join the inverter and NAND without leaving a seam gap or creating a short.
question: What has to match so both power rails continue across the seam?
options: Both cells have the same rail heights and the boundaries touch
Both cells have the same width
Both output pins are on the same track
explanation: The cell width can vary. The row height and power-rail positions must agree at the touching boundaries.
focus: Follow the VPWR and VGND tracks on both sides of the seam.
solution: Keep the inverter at the origin. Set the NAND to X = 13.8 µm and Y = 0 µm. Inspect both shared rails and run the checkpoint.
reflection: Record the initial and final offsets. Explain how a layout can pass within each cell and still leave an open power rail in the assembled row.

title: Speed up a NOR’s rising edge
concept: A NOR pulls up through two PMOS devices in series. Widen both devices to speed up the loaded rising edge without growing the cell.
question: Which devices charge Y when both NOR inputs are low?
options: Only the PMOS controlled by B
explanation: The output charges through both PMOS devices. The test lets B fall while A stays low to isolate the rising edge.
focus: Trace P_STACK between MP_A and MP_B. The PMOS path ends at Y.
tune: Widen both PMOS devices and keep the original horizontal pitch.
solution: Set PMOS stack width to 4 µm. Route the cell, then check the layout-loaded B-to-Y rising delay against 75% of the starter value.
reflection: Record delay and footprint before and after sizing. Explain why a wider PMOS stack speeds this transition.

title: Make a NAND easier to drive
concept: Reduce the charge supplied by the previous stage to input B while keeping the NAND pull-down fast under a 40 fF load.
question: Which measurement includes the charge that B supplies while Y moves?
options: The time integral of current from the B source divided by its voltage swing
The capacitance of the output fixture alone
explanation: The integral over the B transition gives input charge. Dividing by the input swing gives effective switched input capacitance for this vector.
focus: Compare MP_B and MN_B. Both load B, but the NMOS sets the width of one transistor in the series pull-down.
tune: Reduce B’s PMOS width first, then vary its NMOS width while watching the 120 ps limit.
solution: Try B PMOS at 1 µm and B NMOS at 1.8 µm. Compare effective input capacitance to the fixed starter and rerun the four truth-table vectors.
reflection: Record input capacitance and loaded delay before and after. Explain how moving one width changed the load seen by the preceding stage.

title: Keep a mux output steady during switching
concept: When both data inputs agree, select should leave the output steady. Size the output inverter to reject an explicit select-to-output coupling stress in the fixture.
question: When should a transition on select leave Y unchanged?
options: Whenever A and B are equal
explanation: Either mux path then selects the same value. A transient excursion is a glitch even when the settled logic is correct.
focus: Follow the paths into SELECTED and locate the final output inverter. The test adds 8 fF of coupling from select to Y.
tune: Increase the output NMOS and PMOS widths independently and compare both equal-input windows.
solution: Try final-stage NMOS at 2 µm and PMOS at 4 µm. Measure the peak absolute excursion around both select edges for each common input level.
reflection: Record both worst-case excursions. Explain why the truth-table samples alone cannot reveal a brief peak.

title: Build a buffer for four loads
concept: Choose sizes for a two-stage non-inverting buffer driving four actual SKY130 inverter inputs. Split the width budget between its first and second stages.
question: Why can sizing up the output stage eventually stop improving total delay?
options: Its gates increase the load on the first stage
Its load changes from four inverters to one
explanation: A larger output stage drives the load harder, but its gates are a larger capacitive load for the first stage.
focus: Trace A through MID to Y. The fixture connects Y to A on each of four identical inverters.
tune: Start with a smaller first stage and wider second stage. Compare both edge delays and the sum of all four widths.
solution: Try first-stage NMOS/PMOS at 1/2 µm and output-stage NMOS/PMOS at 1.5/3 µm. Check both arcs and the 8 µm budget.
reflection: Record both delays and the total width. Explain how you chose where to spend the available width.

title: Build a lower-energy XOR
concept: Walk through 00, 01, 11 and 10 in a loop. Reduce mean energy drawn from the cell’s supply per output transition while limiting all four propagation delays.
question: Why change one XOR input at a time in the energy fixture?
options: Each vector step gives one independent output transition
The supply can then be switched off between steps
The XOR now needs just two truth-table vectors
explanation: A one-bit input change always toggles XOR. Four such steps return the cell to its initial state and give four measurable timing arcs.
focus: Look for the conditional inversion of B and find the internal gate loads before the output stage.
tune: Shrink the internal devices first. Leave enough output-stage drive to keep all four timing arcs within budget.
solution: Try internal NMOS at 0.7 µm and PMOS at 1.4 µm, and output NMOS/PMOS at 1.25/2.5 µm. Check the energy and worst of all four arcs.
reflection: Record energy per transition and worst delay. Explain why the fixture integrates supply current over a full cycle.

title: Find a flip-flop’s setup and hold limits
concept: Sweep D around a rising clock edge. Find the setup and hold limits where captured Q stays valid and clock-to-Q remains within 10% of a settled reference.
question: Which edges move in the setup and hold experiments?
options: D rises before the clock for setup and falls after the clock for hold
The clock falls earlier in both tests
D is held constant in both tests
explanation: The setup sweep reduces how long D is high before the clock. The hold sweep reduces how long it stays high after that edge.
focus: Find the input transmission gate of the master latch. Clock phase controls when D stops reaching the latch.
tune: If the sweep cannot bracket a limit, compare the settled Q reference with the failing rows. Try a different master-input gate size.
solution: Use the default master-input dimensions first. In Timing sweep, work from the settled reference toward the clock. For each sweep report the nearest stable passing row and its adjacent failing offset.
reflection: Record the closest stable passing offset and its adjacent failing offset for setup and hold. Explain the 10% delay criterion and why the result is a bracket.

title: Lay out a half-adder with shared logic
concept: Use one shared NAND term for the half-adder carry and the two intermediate sum gates. Route both outputs and meet both timing limits in a narrower row.
question: Which node should the sum and carry paths reuse?
options: The complement of A AND B
The ground rail as a logic term
explanation: The shared NAND of A and B feeds the sum construction, and an inverter turns it into carry.
focus: Find NAB, the shared NAND output. CO is carry and Y is sum.
measure: In Samples verify both outputs. In Waveforms follow the four sum edges and the carry rise and fall.
tune: Reduce the horizontal pitch to shrink the common row without changing the schematic.
solution: Set horizontal pitch to 5.8 µm. Route VPWR, Y, and CO. Verify both outputs and the row width in Results.
reflection: Record the two delays and width. Explain which gate the sum and carry share and where the area is saved.

title: Build a Schmitt-trigger input
concept: Size the feedback devices in a six-transistor CMOS Schmitt inverter so a slow input sees two distinct switching thresholds.
question: Which voltages define hysteresis here?
options: Input voltage on the upward sweep and input voltage on the downward sweep
explanation: Read the input voltage when output crosses half the supply on each sweep. The difference is hysteresis.
focus: Trace MN_FB and MP_FB from Y to the internal stacked nodes.
measure: Find both half-output crossings on the slow input. Read A at those times; the difference is the hysteresis width.
tune: Increase feedback NMOS and PMOS strength independently. Keep both switching thresholds inside the usable input range.
solution: Try 1 µm for feedback NMOS and 2 µm for feedback PMOS. Check the two switching points and hysteresis target.
reflection: Record both thresholds and explain how the previous output state changes the next input threshold.

title: Build a tri-state bus driver
concept: Lay out a noninverting tri-state buffer. Verify driven high and low, released-bus leakage, and a break-before-make handoff to a second driver.
question: Why does the fixture weakly pull the released bus in both directions?
options: To show that the disabled driver does not force either logic level
To make the output drive more strongly
explanation: A released output follows the weak pull in both directions. The voltage drop across that resistor measures off-state current.
focus: Follow EN and EN_B to the series gating transistors and find the shared Y conductor.
measure: Read the first two sample slots for weak pull-up and pull-down. In the last part of the trace, check the bus when the second driver takes over.
tune: Widen the series output devices while retaining both enable paths and the high-impedance state.
solution: Try 2 µm for both series NMOS devices and 3 µm for both series PMOS devices. Recheck drive delay, both off-state samples, and the handoff.
reflection: Record the released-bus current and the delay. Explain why steady high and low tests would miss a driver that never releases the bus.
